records.title: Show HN: Open Components – UI Components standard for people, devs and AI agents
records.author: alexgrozav
records.storyText:
Hello awesome people,

I've been thinking a lot lately about how I can make my knowledge and craft more valuable in the times we live in. I've been building UI libraries for the past 10 years, and I've been on a quest to perfect the components that I build. I want to share my knowledge with you. Like most of you, probably, I've been using a lot of AI in my craft, and I feel most of the time the code is just good enough, but never at the level of quality that I strive for or that I would reach if I wrote it by hand. That needs to change, and I want it to change for everyone else, too. That's how the Open Components initiative was born.

Each component gets a single page that walks through four directions: User Interface, User Experience, Developer Experience, and Agentic Experience, and ends with a checklist. Every rule in it has an ID like `button/keep-focus`, a level and a way to check it, so you or your agents can cite it in a code review. Every page is also published as markdown, and provides the contract as a YAML file, containing every rule in about an eighth of the page’s length.

It’s still early. Right now there are only the Button and Input components and a page on how to name your design tokens. Each component comes with a reference implementation that meets every rule, along with its tests. Reference implementation is in Vue for now, since that’s my daily driver, but the documentation comes with code examples from multiple UI frameworks. More components will follow, with the same structure.

It isn’t a component library, so there’s nothing to install. It’s a set of rules you can hold your own components to, whichever library or framework you use.

I’d love your feedback and contribution. Tell me what you think of the rules, what I’ve missed, and which component you’d like to see next.

Thanks for reading!

Site: https://opencomponents.dev Button: https://opencomponents.dev/docs/components/button GitHub: https://github.com/uxfront-com/open-components

records.title: Show HN: Coolphabets – Teaching kids to read and write in their mother tongue
records.author: samdung
records.storyText:
COOL + ALPHABETS = COOLPHABETS

COOLPHABETS teaches you to read and write in your mother tongue - for kids who are just starting, and adults who never did.

Millions of families live outside the country they were born in. While parents can read and write in their native language, their kids - the second generation - can barely do so.

Kids often speak their mother tongue fluently because it is the language they use at home. But reading and writing is rarely a "felt need" for them. And kids are unlikely to feel that need unless parents nudge them - preferably at an early age.

Many parents genuinely want their kids to be able to read and write in their mother tongue. This usually means a textbook or a weekend language class. Both can feel like a chore.

Most language apps teach you to 'speak' a language. COOLPHABETS teaches you to 'read' and 'write'. Reading and writing are a genuinely difficult problem to solve - especially on an app. Getting a child to write letters correctly is the harder part.

That's where we built CoolphaSense - a collection of tiny AI models that run entirely on the device and provide instant feedback on handwriting.

COOLPHABETS is designed for kids. No ads. No tracking. COPPA compliant. The apps are designed to work fully offline. No cloud roundtrips to a 'Mothership AI model'.

COOLPHABETS is currently available in Indian languages.

- Telugu - Kannada - Hindi - Tamil - Marathi

Most other Indian languages will be onboarded by December 2026. Other world languages (Asian, Middle Eastern, European) are early next year.

The bigger motivation is cultural. A language can survive for several generations as a spoken language, but if its script is lost, something important is lost with it. If one generation stops reading and writing in its native script, reconnecting with that part of the culture becomes much harder.

If you are a parent who feels this way, COOLPHABETS is for you and your kids.

https://coolphabets.com/

Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.coolphabet...

iPhone: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/coolphabets/id6762379998

We would love to hear from parents settled outside their native countries, parents raising kids in multilingual households, and from people working on handwriting recognition, on-device AI/ML, and language learning.

records.title: Show HN: Peer-to-peer instant messaging with proof-of-work spam protection
records.author: iljah
records.storyText:
Bitmessage.org still doesn't support Python 3 and over the years I've tried several times to create something similar but each time have run up against unclear/incomplete/missing documentation in Python/Rust/flask/tokio/asyncio/etc. Finally decided to give ChatGPT a real try and with tutoring based on minimal examples managed to have something usable in about a day. Most "difficult" part was having two instances of flask/quart running simultaneously while also having other stuff happen periodically in background.

Novel thing in p2pIM compared to Bitmessage is that messages' PoW decays and that larger messages require better PoW than smaller ones. Thus small messages that are discarded quickly require significantly less PoW than large messages that persist for a long time. p2pIM doesn't support encryption but that should be straightforward to build on top.

Message_v0 class in https://github.com/iljah/p2pIM/blob/main/messages.py defines low level details such as PoW, how many bytes to use for nonce, checksum, etc. Currently they're all only about 10 bytes or hex characters for easier debugging and testing. PoW is calculated as sha256 of timestamp+nonce+checksum, where checksum is sha256 of payload. Adding channel name as fourth item to PoW is on the https://github.com/iljah/p2pIM/blob/main/TODO list. server1.py mentioned at end of README is my previous attempt at this (without AI help) and the one before that is probably https://github.com/iljah/a2amd in Rust.

records.title: Show HN: SqlFlow – Durable Workflows Backed by PostgreSQL or SQL Server
records.author: bytefish
records.storyText:
Hey HN!

I have built SqlFlow, which is an open-source durable workflow engine backed by PostgreSQL or SQL Server, with SDKs for .NET, Java, Python, and Go. Workflows support retries, checkpoints, rate limitng, scheduling, and suspension while waiting for events.

It took a large deal of inspiration from Absurd, but it expands on the core concepts.

Instead of polling the database, it supports native database features such as PostgreSQL LISTEN / NOTIFY, SQL Server Service Broke, and you could also use NATS. The durable state always remains in your SQL database.

Each SDK comes with a complete example, that models an AI Agent Workflow:

- https://github.com/bytefish/SqlFlow/tree/main/sdks

I would love to hear your feedback.

records.title: Show HN: PodcastDelay – an open source RSS feed generator
records.author: samcolson42
records.storyText:
I'm a bit nostalgic. There are some podcasts I started listening to years ago (2017~), but not at the start (2008~). At a certain point, the podcast changes, maybe some stalwarts rotate out of the main line-up... I just want to go back, to the beginning.

I'm also someone that has no self-restraint. I'll mainline ten of the same podcast in a day, then forget all about listening to no.11. Podcasts apps do not help this: It's hard to get them to cooperate in a way which surfaces your next episode in the 'Latest episodes' list, because while it may be up next for you, it was actually released 15 years ago.

PodcastDelay solves that, by taking that original feed and 'delaying' it by however long you want. It's a solution for re-publishing a podcast's RSS feed as a new private feed. It can start releasing from any episode, at any cadence, including mirroring the original release cadence.

If a show has two feeds — the regular one and a premium/bonus one — you can merge them into a single delayed feed. Each bonus episode comes out the same distance after its free counterpart as it did originally: an hour stays an hour, a day stays a day, whatever cadence you're replaying the free feed at.

Audio isn't hosted/reposted, but there are plenty of solutions if you wanted to have 'local' media turned into an RSS feed, which PodcastDelay could then put out in the correct cadence.

records.title: Show HN: BraiNOTES, handwritten notes on your lecture PDFs in a browser tab
records.author: swimmingbrain
records.storyText:
In August, I posted here about TeXbrain, a LaTeX editor that runs completely in the browser, with no need for an account or server. (I didn't excpect it to get that much feedback, bug reports and help from here!)

This is the same idea for the other half of my studies, the handwritten notes. I take them on a convertible laptop, and I've had a hard time with apps for that, taking notes from a device to another, exporting as PDF, needing an account for many of them, etc. So I've been working on the version of it that I always wanted. Open a tab, the slides of the lecture or multiple PDFs open next to the page or even become the page, write on them with my pen, and nothing ever leaves my browser.

braiNOTES is a static website and has no backend. Strokes are perfect-freehand outlines which support pen pressure, the PDF files are rendered by pdf.js in a worker, and for storage it uses IndexedDB a moment after every change. No account, no analytics, and completely offline and local-first. You can export notebooks as .brainotes files, which in the background is a zip with one json per page + the PDFs and pictures you import. It keeps the original pages and puts the vectorized ink on top, this way the text stays selectable in the slides.

You can try it here: https://notes.swimmingbrain.dev GitHub Repo: https://github.com/swimmingbrain/brainotes (MIT)

In Study mode, the PDF opens on the side of the tab, you can read it simultaneously to the notes, snip a formula or diagrams directly into the notes with the snip tool, and then write around it. In Board mode, you have just a Whiteboard for tutoring or simply for more place for exercises, and can also highlight or draw things with the laser pointer tool while presenting.

The line of the ink appears the moment the pen moves, and a one euro filter calms shaky hands while you write + a light a refit when you lift the pen.

I also have a video editor and an animation tool which are still a work in progress, on the same GitHub profile. I'm also working on a MCP server for each tool, so you can use your MCP client to do further things with your notes, automatically edit videos on the video editor, etc. That feature will of course be off unless you turn it on and will only be able to talk to localhost.

I've used this tool for every lecture in the last few months and a few friends use it too. Bug reports, fixes, recommendations, feedback are all welcome!

records.title: Show HN: Tessary – Find the AI agent failures your sampled evals miss
records.author: infinitetrooper
records.storyText:
Hey, I'm Akhil, co-founder of Tessary. An open-source agent reliability platform that monitors every production trace, detects issues that sampled evals miss, and investigates to find the root cause.

We started up about a year ago building synthetic users for usability testing of B2B software, we built the agents that would personify real users and use the software but, we were never able to make them work reliably enough for long running sessions. We had built a massive eval set to tune our agents but, then the evaluation itself got prohibitively costly - like 5x costlier than actually running the agent since we needed to grade across the many narrow intents of our agent. That's where Tessary originated, we wanted to make agent reliability both cover more ground and be simultaneously less costly to run.

Tessary works on 2 layers.

L1 classifiers - which look at every agent trace and flag potentially erroneous ones extremely cheaply. We are talking 2-3 orders of magnitude cheaper than running the actual agent.

L2 agents - which triage and find the root cause of the issue from the erroneous traces. These are run on SOTA models but, because we run them on already flagged traces, the time and $ spent finding the cause is much cheaper than running grading on even 1% of traces. In our testing on complex agents, at 1M traces, this approach was 5x cheaper than sampled evaluations and as your agent gets more reliable, the cost of reliability also goes down.

we are open source and can be self-hosted so, you don't need to send your traces to us. We support existing `gen_ai` spec and ingestion over OTLP so, you can add this as a new exporter to your existing setup. We have a cloud version, you can quickly try the features with a $10 credit.

We are looking to build more classifiers and enable people to build custom classifiers for their needs and would love to hear feedback on common failure modes people have built solutions or evaluation for

Repo: https://github.com/tessaryai/tessary Website: https://tessary.ai Try for free: https://app.tessary.ai

Hi HN,

I built AntiPDF, a native PDF reader AND editor for Windows (coming to Linux and MacOS). I built it because I got tired of getting ads and all those Acrobatics.

AntiPDF can read, edit, annotate, OCR and organize PDFs while keeping your documents on your computer. It's written completely in Odin and rendered with Vulkan using MSDF fonts for those lovely smooth fonts.

Any action in the program that took longer than 20ms was questioned and rewritten. The "Anti" isn't about PDFs. It's to highlight and be against an industry of capitalistic habits that users have learned to tolerate. The program has a paying part but that is because I have to pay for storage if you choose that option. For reading and "Editing" PDFs you don't need to pay. And you will never see ads just because you accidentally clicked a button.

Happy to answer questions about the implementation, PDF internals, Odin, Vulkan, or the product itself.

records.title: Show HN: Lacuna – open-source inline AI writing suggestions for your Mac
records.author: jdamon96
records.storyText:
This past week I built (prompted) a tool I find myself using day to day and wanted to share it with others who may find it useful as well.

“Lacuna” is an opinionated way to invoke LLMs into any text input on your Mac. Specifically, you can type bracketed phrases {such as this}, press Shift-Command-K (or a different shortcut of your choosing), and the tool sends your bracketed phrase + the surrounding text contents to an LLM of your configuration for generating text to replace the bracketed phrase. The program returns 3 candidate phrases and the experience is entirely keyboard navigable.

Demo: https://jackdamon.org/assets/images/lacuna-scheduling-demo.g...

Example scheduling workflow using Lacuna’s native UI and sample suggestions.

So far I find myself frequently using it when drafting emails where I want help with quick phrasing.

The project was inspired by Rectangle, an open source utility app for window tiling that is keyboard based.

records.title: Show HN: Context Diet – trims tool output before it floods Claude Code's context
records.author: hy4hy
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I built this after watching long Claude Code sessions fill up with tool output: a single verbose test run or build log can be 30–50k characters, almost all of it PASSED lines, warnings and lockfile churn. The context fills, compaction comes sooner, and the agent forgets earlier instructions.

Context Diet is a mod (Claude Code's new JS hook API) that rewrites tool results before they are stored in the conversation:

- test runners and build tools (jest, vitest, pytest, go test, cargo, tsc, eslint, npm/pip install, docker build) get parsed digests: every failure with its message and location, plus the summary; passing tests are counted, not listed - JSON becomes a skeleton, diffs drop lockfile churn, grep results and file lists are grouped, tables keep exact first and last rows - running the same command again shows only what changed - the full output is always saved to a file, and the digest says where, so the agent can read it when it needs more

The question I cared about most was whether it makes the agent worse. On 7 Q&A tasks with known answers, both groups were 7/7, with 8 tool calls instead of 13. On a bug-fixing task (600 tests, two hidden bugs, Haiku/Sonnet/Opus, 18 runs) every agent fixed both bugs with or without it, using 6 tool calls instead of 8.

Honest caveats: the token saving on very large outputs is modest, because Claude Code already moves those to a file; the gain there is fewer steps. Also, when a command fails, Claude Code keeps only ~10k characters and drops the end of the output, where the failures usually are. There is an opt-in mode that saves the whole output first, off by default because it changes the command text.

It's MIT, makes no network calls, and I'd love examples of output it digests badly.

records.title: Show HN: Higherlevel – Define and review what AI agents build
records.author: cyan_indigo
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

I'm Ryan, I'm building Higherlevel (https://higherlevel.to) so product teams have one place to define and review software changes.

Over the last couple of years, I've been increasingly delegating software implementation to AI coding agents.

However, because it became easier and faster to ship complexity, I realised that it still takes me quite some time to even understand what the software is doing, why it is doing that, or review the changes.

I also don't do traditional code reviews anymore, it's mostly automated but I still want to review the final outcome of the changes (rather than its implementation).

I regularly work on complex B2B applications where a single feature can involve dozen of business rules, edge cases and interactions with existing functionality.

I found myself spending more and more time discovering and explaining requirements to agents, reviewing their output, asking for evdience and trying to establish whether we actually agreed on what correct behaviour looked like.

So I built Higherlevel. The idea is to bring product specifications and proof of work into a single collaborative workspace.

You can: - describe the current behaviour, known limitations and expected changes - define business rules, acceptance scenarios using Given/When/Then - demand evidence in the form of a screenshot, a video, etc - comment directly on the spec, on a specific area of the image or a timestamp of the video - discuss changes, track revisions and approve results with your team

I've written extensively about why I believe in specification driven development (and what it means to me) here https://higherlevel.to/blog/introducing-higherlevel

Higherlevel is currently in beta and built with Elixir, Phoenix LiveView, and PostgreSQL.
